title: Microscopically informed self-consistent multi-resolvent closure for dense many-body spectra
abstract: The exact multi-resolvent hierarchy of dense many-body spectra encodes higher-order spectral-weight correlations, but closing it predictively for interacting Hamiltonians remains a challenge. We introduce the multi-resolvent self-consistency (MRSC) equations, which separate an exact algebraic hierarchy from an approximate finite-parameter closure. The exact Feshbach geometric identity organizes r-resolvent cumulants into a ladder over irreducible vertices Gamma^(r), and the projected hierarchy expresses those vertices as functionals of the cumulants. The closure works in finite parameters: a connectivity basis organizes a general Hamiltonian's seed into class amplitudes, and a causal r-fold Stieltjes representation with a moment-field identity reduce moment matching to a finite-dimensional problem closed at a predictive fixed point. On the free-fermion benchmark the tested exact identities are reproduced and the Faddeeva closure is recovered at r=1. In a blind test on the interacting Ising chain, with the exact two-resolvent data withheld, the Hamiltonian-derived closure predicts the tested probes to 0.35%-0.97%. At the observable level the exact two-resolvent sector supplies a sign-correct, energy-resolved correction to the single-resolvent baseline for the off-diagonal eigenstate-thermalization-hypothesis (ETH) variance, of order one relative to it. Closure errors organize hierarchically: a level-by-level deficit decomposition, anchor measurements of the isolatable terms, and an explicit propagation bound. The same moments further yield a diagnostic chain for the window conditions of local rotational invariance -- an exact drift-kernel identity, a proven single-state identifiability boundary, and a transferability census over couplings and realizations -- a finite-order framework, not a proof of universal emergence.
summary: This work introduces the Multi-Resolvent Self-Consistency (MRSC) equations to tackle the intractable problem of high-order spectral correlations in many-body systems. By creating a finite, predictive closure based on exact identities, the authors provide a powerful tool to calculate spectral properties, notably improving the understanding of thermalization dynamics beyond single-resolvent approximations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing a finite, predictive closure for the exact, high-order multi-resolvent hierarchy that describes dense many-body spectral correlations.
main_result: The proposed Multi-Resolvent Self-Consistency (MRSC) framework successfully predicts spectral probes on the interacting Ising chain with high accuracy and provides a sign-correct correction to the ETH variance.
method: It introduces MRSC equations that separate an exact algebraic hierarchy from a finite-parameter closure, utilizing the Feshbach identity and moment-field identities to constrain the problem.
model_or_system: The theory is tested on free-fermion and interacting Ising chain models, focusing on general interacting Hamiltonians defined on a Hilbert space spanned by a product basis.
key_observables: Energy-resolved spectral cumulants, off-diagonal eigenstate-thermalization-hypothesis (ETH) variance, and local rotational invariance diagnostics.
important_parameters: The closure is parameterized by a finite set of self-consistent parameters ($	heta$) derived from moment matching.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the validity of the causal $r$-fold Stieltjes representation and relies on truncating the infinite hierarchy to a finite, self-consistent set of parameters.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the MRSC architecture flow chart, detailing the path from the microscopic Hamiltonian to the self-consistent spectral parameters and error analysis.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the exact algebraic hierarchy using the Feshbach identity, then developing the MRSC equations to enforce a finite-parameter closure via moment matching, and finally validating this closure against known benchmarks and diagnostic tests.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, computable framework to analyze spectral correlations and thermalization properties in interacting quantum systems, bridging the gap between exact spectral theory and practical, finite-parameter calculations.
